source: Instantaneous Velocity
The velocity at an instant is the slope of the tangent line to the x–t graph.
Students think an object at x = 0 must have zero velocity, mixing up position with velocity.
A speedometer shows your velocity right now, not over a trip. On a curved position-time graph the slope keeps changing, so we need the slope at a single point.
The instantaneous velocity at time $t$ is the slope of the tangent line to the $x$–$t$ graph at $t$: the line that just touches the curve there and runs in the same direction.

Take the average velocity over a short interval around $t$, then a shorter one, then shorter still. On a smooth curve, zooming in makes the curve look straighter and straighter, and those average-velocity lines settle down to one line: the tangent. Its slope is the velocity at that instant. In calculus this is the derivative, but the idea only needs slopes.
A ball rolling up a ramp and back: x = 1 + 6t − t². The tangent is flat at t = 3 s, where the ball turns around.
The same motion with its cart. The dashed tangent on the x–t graph has the slope shown on the v–t graph at the same moment.
Worked examples
The tangent to an $x$–$t$ curve at $t = 2\ \text{s}$ passes through $(1\ \text{s}, 4\ \text{m})$ and $(3\ \text{s}, 8\ \text{m})$. Find the velocity at $t = 2\ \text{s}$.
From a tangent line
$2\ \text{m/s}$
Slope $= \dfrac{8 - 4}{3 - 1} = \dfrac{4\ \text{m}}{2\ \text{s}}$.
$v = 2\ \text{m/s}$.
A sensor reads $x = 5.39\ \text{m}$ at $t = 2.9\ \text{s}$ and $x = 5.79\ \text{m}$ at $t = 3.1\ \text{s}$. Estimate the velocity at $t = 3\ \text{s}$.
From a short interval
about $2.0\ \text{m/s}$
Over this short interval, $v \approx \dfrac{5.79 - 5.39}{3.1 - 2.9} = \dfrac{0.40}{0.2}$.
$v \approx 2.0\ \text{m/s}$. A shorter interval would give an even better estimate.

Thinking an object at $x = 0$ must have zero velocity. Position and velocity are different questions: a car passing the origin at highway speed is at $x = 0$ with a large velocity, and a ball at the top of its rise has zero velocity far from the origin. Check: velocity comes from the slope of the graph, never from its height.
